title: Baahubali Is Going to Annecy. India's $400 Crore Animated Gamble Just Crashed the Cannes of Cartoons.
excerpt: Tickets for the Eternal War work-in-progress panel sold out in two minutes flat. For the first time, the world's most prestigious animation festival is making room for Mahishmati.
body:
It took two minutes. That is how long the tickets to the Baahubali: The Eternal War work-in-progress panel lasted once bookings opened at the Annecy International Animation Film Festival — gone before most of the room had finished their morning coffee. For an Indian animated film that almost nobody outside the country has seen a frame of, in front of the most exacting animation crowd on earth, that is not a footnote. That is a statement.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=iDqSKfIQ-q4

Annecy is the room. Held this year from June 21 to 27 in the French Alps, it is the festival they call the Cannes of animation, and its Work in Progress strand is where the future gets auditioned. Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse previewed there. So did Flow, the dialogue-free Latvian wonder that walked off with the 2025 Academy Award for Best Animated Feature. To be selected into that lineup — twelve features, three series and one immersive project from ten countries — is to be told you belong in serious company. And S. S. Rajamouli, the man who made the world care about Mahishmati, is the one presenting it.

"I have always believed animation offers a canvas with no boundaries. It is a rare honor for Indian mainstream cinema that 'Baahubali: The Eternal War' has been selected for the Work in Progress lineup at Annecy 2026." — S. S. Rajamouli

Let's be clear about what this film actually is, because it is not a recap. The Eternal War is a two-part animated continuation of the saga, picking up the thread after Baahubali 2: The Conclusion and launching it somewhere no live-action budget could follow — a mythological afterlife where Amarendra Baahubali is drawn into a cosmic war between the Devas and the Asuras. The story stretches across fourteen mystical realms, a scale that frankly only animation can render without collapsing under its own ambition. This is the franchise doing what the franchise always did: refusing to think small.

The pedigree is stacked. Prabhas returns to voice Amarendra, the role that turned him into a pan-India deity, and Ramya Krishnan is back as well — you cannot have Mahishmati without Sivagami. The film is directed by Ishan Shukla, written by Shukla with Sowmya Sharma, with screenplay duties handed to Scott Mosier (yes, the Grinch and Kevin Smith collaborator) and dialogues by Deva Katta and Madhan Karky. Academy Award winner M. M. Keeravaani, fresh off the global victory lap of Naatu Naatu, is scoring it. Producers Shobu Yarlagadda and Prasad Devineni are mounting it under Arka Mediaworks on a reported budget north of ₹120 crore, with international collaborators brought in to hit a 3D standard that can stand next to Pixar and Sony without flinching.

That last part is the real test, and everyone involved knows it. Indian animation has spent years trapped in a reputation for cut-rate kids' content, the stuff that plays on weekday-morning television and nowhere else. The Eternal War is a deliberate, expensive bid to break that ceiling — to prove that a homegrown studio can deliver theatrical, adult, mythologically dense animation that the rest of the world will pay to watch. The teaser has already racked up serious international buzz. Annecy is where the industry decides whether the rest of the film can cash that cheque.

For the diaspora, this is the kind of story that hits twice. There is the obvious pride — an Indian epic earning a marquee slot at the world's animation high table, the same stage that launched Oscar winners. But there is also the practical hope. The makers are planning to release the first part in 2027, and a film built from the ground up for global standards, in a wordless-friendly visual language and backed by a Rajamouli name that already opens doors in North America, is precisely the sort of Indian project that could get a real theatrical and streaming push across the US, UK and Canada — not a token one-week run, but a genuine release. NRI parents who grew up on Baahubali now have kids of their own to pass it down to. An animated chapter is how a legend becomes a bedtime story.

Whether The Eternal War lives up to the teaser is a question for 2027. But the sold-out-in-two-minutes panel at Annecy answers a different one already: the world is curious about what India can do when it stops filming reality and starts drawing it. Jai Mahishmati, indeed.
